subject: AI & Digital Construction
author: Anthony Hammond
title: AI in Construction: Innovation Without Losing Engineering Judgement
subHeading: Why the real opportunity lies in connecting people, models and information rather than replacing engineering expertise.
abstract: AI is changing construction, but impressive outputs don't necessarily mean good engineering. Explore the limitations of AI, the importance of engineering judgement, and why properly coordinated BIM workflows and accessible project information may offer the industry's greatest opportunity.
body:
Artificial intelligence is moving quickly, and the construction industry is no exception. From automated design and model generation to document analysis and intelligent data management, the possibilities are exciting. Tasks that once took hours can now be completed in minutes, and information that was previously difficult to access is becoming increasingly easy to retrieve.

But amid all the excitement, I think we need to take a step back and ask a more fundamental question: just because AI can produce something, does that mean we should trust it?

## Looking Beyond the Surface

Take this website, for example. It looks good, doesn't it? The design does its job, the information is accessible, and it provides a platform for presenting my work.

But beneath the surface, some of the software engineering is far from ideal.

AI has helped me develop parts of this website much faster than I could have done working entirely on my own. With a reasonable understanding of programming, I can describe what I want, review the output, identify problems and work towards a solution. The result is something functional, even if the underlying code could be considerably cleaner, more efficient and easier to maintain.

Is that necessarily a disaster? Not at this stage.

If a layout breaks or a component fails to render correctly, I can investigate the problem, modify the code and get things working again. There are certainly risks associated with poorly structured software, but the consequences of a misaligned element on a blog page are generally limited. The world isn't going to fall apart because a heading isn't centred correctly.

For my current purposes, the website serves its intended function. I can accept some technical debt while I continue to develop it, provided I understand the compromises I'm making and address the important problems as the project grows.

However, there is a distinction here that I think is particularly important.

A product that looks impressive is not necessarily a product that has been engineered well.

If you don't understand programming, it can be difficult to recognise the difference. AI can produce something visually convincing, demonstrate a working feature and give the impression that a complex problem has been solved. Yet underneath that polished exterior, the code might contain unnecessary complexity, hidden assumptions, security vulnerabilities or fundamental architectural problems.

The same principle applies far beyond software. An impressive-looking output is not proof that the process behind it is reliable.

And this is where we need to start thinking differently about AI in construction.

## When the Consequences Change

Now consider the same approach applied to civil or structural engineering.

Imagine using AI to generate a drainage design, calculate reinforcement requirements or assist with the design of a structural connection. The output might look perfectly reasonable. The drawings might be professionally presented, the calculations might appear convincing, and the model might look exactly as you would expect.

But what happens if the assumptions are wrong? What if a critical load case has been overlooked, a design constraint has been misunderstood, or a calculation contains an error that isn't immediately obvious?

In software development, some mistakes are relatively inexpensive to correct. In civil engineering, an undetected mistake can have consequences far beyond the drawing or model in which it originated. Depending on the application, it can contribute to structural failure, flooding, unsafe construction or loss of life.

This doesn't mean AI has no place in engineering. It means that the standard of evidence we require must reflect the consequences of getting something wrong.

We cannot judge an engineering application of AI by how convincing its output looks, how quickly it produces an answer or how impressed we are by the demonstration.

We need to ask whether the result is correct, whether its assumptions are understood, whether it can be independently verified and whether the person responsible has the competence to recognise when something is wrong.

In other words, engineering judgement cannot be replaced by confidence in a tool.

AI can assist with calculations, generate code, suggest design options and help engineers explore problems. But assistance is not the same as verification, and generating an answer is not the same as demonstrating that the answer is safe.

The greater the consequences of an error, the less acceptable it becomes to rely on an output simply because it appears plausible.

## Where AI Can Make a Real Difference

None of this is an argument against AI. Quite the opposite.

I believe there are enormous opportunities for its application across the built environment. The key is identifying where it genuinely adds value, rather than forcing it into every part of the engineering process.

Consider technical documentation. Construction projects generate enormous quantities of information: specifications, contracts, drawings, standards, inspection records, design reports and correspondence. Finding the right piece of information at the right time can be a challenge in itself.

AI-assisted document retrieval, particularly when combined with vector databases and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), offers a way to make this information more accessible. Instead of manually searching through hundreds of pages, a user could ask a question in ordinary language and retrieve relevant passages from approved project documents or technical standards.

Contract analysis, document classification, information extraction and the identification of discrepancies are other promising applications.

These tools can help people find information faster, identify matters requiring attention and reduce the administrative burden associated with complex projects. Their outputs still need appropriate checking, particularly where contractual obligations, technical requirements or safety are concerned, but their value is clear.

## The Real Opportunity: Connecting the Pieces

When we talk about AI in construction, I think we risk becoming too focused on what the technology can produce in isolation. We see demonstrations of AI generating impressive drawings, producing detailed three-dimensional models from a single prompt or automating tasks that previously required specialist knowledge. These capabilities are exciting, but I don't necessarily believe they represent the biggest opportunity for our industry.

For me, the real game changer is getting the construction process right in the digital world before we ever take it to site.

Building Information Modelling has the potential to bring together the different disciplines, datasets and processes involved in delivering a project. Yet the value isn't simply in having a three-dimensional model. It's in how that model connects the design to the information needed to construct, coordinate and ultimately operate the building or infrastructure.

A model can look impressive and still be of limited practical use if the information behind it is incomplete, the different disciplines aren't properly coordinated or the people responsible for construction cannot access what they need. Equally, a relatively straightforward model that is properly structured, coordinated and connected to reliable project information can be enormously valuable.

Think about the people involved in delivering a project. Engineers need to understand the technical design. Architects need to develop spaces that meet the client's requirements. BIM coordinators need to identify and resolve interfaces between disciplines. Site managers need to plan activities, manage resources and make sure work can be carried out safely and efficiently. The people installing the work need clear, accurate and accessible information.

These are different professions with different responsibilities. The objective shouldn't be to replace them with a machine that attempts to do everything. It should be to connect them, giving each person access to the information they need to do their job properly.

Imagine being able to identify a coordination issue while the project is still being developed, understand its implications for construction sequencing, communicate the resolution to the relevant teams and ensure the correct information reaches the people carrying out the work. Imagine being able to interrogate a coordinated model and retrieve the relevant specifications, installation details and design requirements without searching through disconnected systems.

That is where I see enormous potential.

AI may help us search, interpret and navigate this information. Automation can perform repetitive checks, and computational tools can help us explore complex problems. But none of these capabilities removes the need for sound engineering, competent design, effective management or properly coordinated information.

In fact, the better we structure our models, manage our data and connect our workflows, the more useful these technologies are likely to become.

The objective is not to get AI to do everyone's job. It is to give everyone the information and tools they need to do their job better.

I believe this is where we should be concentrating much of our effort: developing digital construction workflows that allow us to understand a project, coordinate its different components and resolve problems before they become expensive or dangerous issues on site.

Build the job properly in the digital world before we build it in the physical one.

That, in my opinion, is the real opportunity. AI can contribute to it, but it shouldn't distract us from the fundamentals of good BIM and good engineering.

## The Question of Data Ownership

There is another issue we need to consider as AI becomes more deeply integrated into construction: who controls the information we give these systems?

Construction projects contain commercially sensitive and sometimes proprietary information. Design models, pricing schedules, construction methodologies, asset data and client documentation can all have significant value.

When we submit this information to an external AI service, we need to understand what happens to it. How is it stored? Who can access it? Is it used to improve models? Where is it processed? What contractual protections apply? Can the information be deleted when the relationship ends?

The answers depend on the provider, the product, the account configuration and the contractual arrangements. It would be wrong to assume that every AI service uses submitted information in the same way. Equally, it would be unwise to assume that uploading information to a platform is risk-free simply because doing so is convenient.

These concerns extend beyond AI itself.

Construction is increasingly dependent on common data environments (CDEs), cloud platforms and proprietary software ecosystems. Such platforms can offer substantial benefits, including collaboration, version control, information management and centralised access. However, organisations also need to consider interoperability, data portability, licensing costs and the practical difficulty of moving to another system.

A project can become heavily dependent on a platform's particular data structures, integrations and workflows. Even when information can technically be exported, transferring it into another environment may require considerable time and effort.

This raises an important question for the future of digital construction: how do we benefit from powerful platforms without surrendering unnecessary control over our data and workflows?

There may be situations where a major commercial platform is the right choice. In others, a more focused custom solution, an open data standard or a combination of different tools may provide greater flexibility.

The answer will depend on the project, the organisation and the requirements involved. But these decisions deserve the same careful consideration as any other technical or commercial decision.

## Moving Forward With Our Eyes Open

AI will almost certainly become an increasingly important part of the construction industry. The opportunity to improve information retrieval, automate repetitive processes, analyse complex datasets and connect digital models with practical construction activities is too significant to ignore.

But adoption for its own sake is not progress.

We need to distinguish between outputs that look impressive and systems that are reliable. We need to understand the limitations of the tools we use, verify their results in proportion to the risks involved, and maintain clear responsibility for engineering decisions.

We also need to think carefully about the information we provide to external services, the platforms on which we depend and the long-term ownership of our digital assets.

Most importantly, we should focus on solving real problems.

If AI helps a site team find the right information, helps a BIM coordinator identify a potential issue before it reaches the construction site, or helps an engineer spend less time searching through documents and more time applying their expertise, then it is doing something genuinely useful.

If it produces an impressive-looking result that nobody understands, nobody verifies and everybody assumes must be correct, then we have a very different problem.

At Hammond BIM Tech, these are questions I want to explore further. From AI-assisted engineering and BIM automation to reinforcement detailing, digital construction workflows, data interoperability and the trade-offs between custom solutions and major software platforms, there is a great deal to investigate.

The technology is moving quickly. Our understanding of how best to use it needs to keep pace.

The question is not whether AI belongs in construction. It is how we use it intelligently, responsibly and in ways that make the industry better.

And that is where the conversation begins.
